_editing: Result cards live in `roles`. The grid lookup lives in `cells`. Badge rules live in `badges`. The four-function definition lives in `definition`. Nothing here is referenced by name in quiz.js except the top-level keys, so you can rewrite any copy freely.

definition._note: The definition the quiz is built on. Quoted as written — do not paraphrase. The X axis scores how much of this a person's habits engage.
definition.statement: Companion AI refers to any AI tool that demonstrates the following four functions: persistent memory, emulated empathy, anthropomorphism, and constant availability.

functions.name: Persistent memory
functions.text: The capacity to retain information disclosed in prior interactions (facts, preferences, emotional history) and to draw on it so that the relationship appears to accumulate over time.

functions.name: Emulated empathy
functions.text: From Andrew McStay: the function of appearing to possess strong human empathy while having only weak empathy, sensing and responding to emotional states without felt experience.

functions.name: Anthropomorphism
functions.text: The function of presenting as human or human-like; through first-person address, a name or persona, a human-like voice, and expressed emotions, such that the user relates to the system as someone rather than something.

functions.name: Constant availability
functions.text: The property of being reachable at any time, without limit on duration or frequency, and without the reciprocal claims that human relationships impose.

definition.beyondDefinition: Sycophancy and proactive relational initiative are scored on the same axis but are not part of the definition. They are flagged `inDefinition: false` below and labelled as additional design functions wherever they appear.

pageFurniture.deck: Answer honestly about how you actually use it. At the end you'll find out which friendship role you've handed to a chatbot — and whether anybody has bothered to study young people doing the same thing.
pageFurniture.pullQuote: Most of the roles on this page have never been studied in anyone your age. That is not a gap in you. It is a gap in the research.
pageFurniture.footerSlug: IS YOUR AI GOOD FOR YOU? · NO ACCOUNTS · NO ANALYTICS · NOTHING LEAVES THIS DEVICE
pageFurniture.timeEstimate: 18 questions · about 4 minutes · saves on this device only
pageFurniture.careNote: One more thing, and then this page is done talking: if any of this is heavier than it looks written down, the person to tell is a person. A friend, a relative, a school counsellor — whoever is nearest to being on your side.

gridLabels.title: Where that puts you
gridLabels.xAxis: Function depth — how much of the companion function set your habits switch on
gridLabels.yAxis: Role depth — how close a friendship role your use occupies

companionnessScale._note: Companionness is a property of the resolved role, not a separate measurement. Each role carries its own value under roles.<key>.companionness. Anchors below are the fixed reference points printed under the meter.
companionnessScale.label: companionness
companionnessScale.caption: How companion-like this pattern of use is. It's a position on a scale, not a score out of anything — nothing here is being marked.

definitionPanel._status: [DRAFT COPY] — heading and lead only; the four function texts under `definition` are not draft
definitionPanel.lead: Companion AI is defined here by four functions. This is how many of them your own habits switch on — a tool can have all four built in, and you can still only use one of them.

breakScreen._note: The single pause screen, shown once at the halfway point. Deliberately flat: no praise, no encouragement, no 'you're doing great'. It says where you are and what the rest is for, and gets out of the way.
breakScreen.heading: Nine down, nine to go.
breakScreen.body: The first half asked what the tool does. The second half asks what you bring it and who hears things first — those are the answers that decide which role comes out at the end.

xBands.name: TOOL MODE
xBands.blurb: You use it and put it down. Almost none of the features built to make a chatbot feel like company are switched on in how you use it.

xBands.name: SOMEWHERE IN BETWEEN
xBands.blurb: Some of the company-shaped features are doing work for you and some aren't. This is where most people land.

xBands.name: THE WHOLE KIT
xBands.blurb: Nearly all of it is switched on for you: it remembers, it's always there, it reacts to how you feel, and it mostly agrees with you.

functions._note: The first four are the definition. Sycophancy and proactive relational initiative are additional design functions the quiz also scores; they carry inDefinition:false and are never presented as part of the definition. `engagedAt` is the score at which a function counts as switched on by someone's habits: 3 of a possible 4, so it takes a clear yes on one question plus a partial on the other. Half (2) was too generous — it let a person who answered in the middle of every question read as engaging three of the four.

cells._note: Result cell = dominant category flag × Y band. Every cell resolves to one named companionship role, so the evidence status and the companionness reading are properties of the role and never of the person answering. The lifelong cell is gated on q17 because Gupta's fourth grade is defined by years of shared memory — depth alone must not be able to reach it.

documented.label: Documented
documented.lead: Other young people are doing this, and somebody measured it.

thin.label: Thin
thin.lead: Some evidence exists, with a catch.

unstudied.label: Unstudied
unstudied.lead: Nobody has actually studied young people using AI this way yet. Which means you know something the researchers don't.

mentor-tutor.name: THE HOMEWORK FRIEND
mentor-tutor.tag: the most common role, and the least examined
mentor-tutor.body: You mostly bring it work. Essays, revision, plans, the thing due tomorrow. That sounds like the boring result and it isn't: helping with schoolwork is the single biggest thing young people use these tools for, which makes this the best-documented role on the whole map. It's also the one almost nobody studies as a *relationship*. Researchers count it as a cheating problem, not a friendship one. And that matters, because tutor is the role through which most young people first form a habit of confiding. It's where the door opens.
mentor-tutor.whatToDo: Next time it explains something well, explain it back to an actual person — someone in your class, a sibling, anyone. Saying it out loud to a human is the part that makes it stick.

receipts.finding: 54% of teens use chatbots for schoolwork — the single largest use recorded. 57% use them for information-seeking.
receipts.context: Pew also notes that majorities of teens report NOT using chatbots for casual conversation or emotional support.

receipts.finding: The tools doing this work are general assistants, not companion apps: ChatGPT reaches 78% of AI-using minors, Character AI 15%, Replika 2%.
receipts.context: Multiple-select question, so these cannot be summed. Fig 5B, p. 14.

mentor-tutor.gap: Treated as benign and therefore almost never studied as a relational role, even though it is the role through which most young people first form a habit of confiding.

confidant.name: THE ONE YOU TELL FIRST
confidant.body: When something happens, this is where it goes first. Not the group chat, not a person — here. In the taxonomy this quiz uses, that's the third grade of friendship: the one built on emotional intimacy and trust. There's real evidence other people your age are doing exactly this, so you are not unusual. The honest catch is in the research itself: nobody has managed to separate teenagers confiding in a chatbot built to be a companion from teenagers confiding in a homework assistant. Same behaviour, and the studies can't tell the two apart yet.
confidant.whatToDo: There's probably one person who'd want to hear the thing you've only typed into a chat. Try them with a small piece of it and see how it goes.

receipts.finding: 31% of minors who had used one of these tools had asked it for help or support about something scary or confusing that happened to them.

33% of teens used AI companions for social interaction and relationships — a category defined as "conversation practice, emotional support, role-playing, friendship, or romantic interactions." 31% found the conversations as satisfying or more satisfying than those with real-life friends.
receipts.context: Countervailing findings from the same survey: 80% reported spending more time with real friends than with AI companions, against 6% reporting the opposite, and two in five had applied a skill practised with AI in real life.

confidant.gap: No instrument separates confiding in a labelled companion from confiding in an assistant, so the paper's central comparison cannot yet be made quantitatively.

romantic-partner.name: THE FLIRT FILE
romantic-partner.tag: the one the lawmakers actually noticed
romantic-partner.body: Some of what you do here is romantic — flirting, roleplay, working out what you'd say to someone real. This is the role that gets nearly all of the attention: almost every law written about AI companions is aimed at this and pretty much nothing else. Two things worth knowing. It's more common than people admit, and there is survey evidence for it. And it's mid-table on the evidence map, not the top — three other roles have as much or more evidence behind them and attract no rules at all. Practising conversations is a real thing that does transfer. It just doesn't finish the job.
romantic-partner.whatToDo: Rehearsal counts, but it only counts once — the transfer happens when you use it on a person. Try the low-stakes version out loud with someone: a conversation, not a confession.

receipts.finding: 31% of minors who had used one of these tools had talked to it or sought advice about romantic feelings or relationships. 11% had flirty, romantic, or sexual conversations.
Nearly 1 in 5 students have had, or have friends who have had, romantic relationships with AI.
receipts.context: The finding is on record but its venue, method and sample size are not, so this receipt is thinner than the others on this card.

romantic-partner.gap: The only role companion-specific regulation reliably targets, and the one where the assistant/companion split in the underlying data is least visible.

therapist-like._status: [DRAFT COPY] — name, tag, body, whatToDo. Care-sensitive cell: copy must stay warm, must mention a trusted person, must not read as an alarm and must not list crisis hotlines.
therapist-like.name: THE 3 A.M. LISTENER
therapist-like.body: The hard days go into the chat. Panic, low patches, the stuff you'd technically take to a counsellor if getting one were easy. A lot of people your age do this and there's solid evidence for it, so nothing about this result is a verdict on you. What's worth knowing is the mismatch: the rules that require a chatbot to react properly when someone is struggling were written for apps that call themselves companions. The general-purpose assistants — the ones actually doing most of this work — mostly aren't covered. So the tool getting your worst nights is often the one with the fewest requirements attached to it.
therapist-like.whatToDo: Late nights are the hardest time to think straight, and a chat window is always the easiest door to open. Pick one person you trust — a friend, a relative, a school counsellor — and tell them a smaller version of it in daylight.

receipts.finding: 29% of minors who had used one of these tools sought help or support about something scary or confusing that happened to someone else. Separately, 15% of minors who had experienced online sexual harm sought advice from an AI chatbot or companion afterwards — more than twice the rate at which they turned to some other sources.
receipts.context: Fig 5C, p. 15, plus Thorn's disclosure chapter.

receipts.finding: 48.7% of adults with a mental health condition use large language models for mental health support.
receipts.context: This figure is about adults, not teenagers, and comes from a trade magazine summarising other studies rather than from a primary study.

therapist-like.gap: Crisis-response requirements exist in California S.B. 243 but apply to the companion category, not to the assistants doing most of this work.

casual-friend.name: THE HANGOUT HABIT
casual-friend.tag: the most common relational use, barely researched
casual-friend.body: Nothing heavy. You open it when you're bored, you talk about whatever, you close it. In friendship terms that's the second grade: built on shared interests or just passing time, and usually there for a specific purpose. Here's the odd part. This is probably the most common way young people relate to these tools, and it's the least researched of the lot — because it doesn't produce a dramatic story, so nobody funds a study on it. The evidence that exists is real but thin, and it mostly arrives secondhand.
casual-friend.whatToDo: Pick one thing you'd normally type into the chat this week and text it to a friend instead. Small boring stuff counts — that's most of what a friendship is actually made of.

receipts.finding: 16% of teens have used chatbots to have casual conversations.
receipts.context: Pew notes majorities of teens report not doing this; information-seeking (57%) and schoolwork (54%) remain the dominant uses.

receipts.finding: 30% of teens cite entertainment and curiosity as a reason for using AI companions. 9% say it is easier to talk to AI than to people.
receipts.context: These figures come via Teen Vogue's reporting of the Common Sense Media survey rather than the report itself — a reliable route to the numbers and an unreliable one to the definitions.

casual-friend.gap: The most common relational use and the least theorised, because it produces no dramatic harm and so attracts no research funding.

acquaintance.name: THE BACKGROUND BUDDY
acquaintance.body: It's around, you use it, it isn't a big deal to you. That's the thinnest grade of friendship in the taxonomy — the person you see constantly and never go deep with, giving you a bit of belonging without much depth. A chatbot fits that description almost perfectly, and here's the thing: nobody has measured it. Not because it's rare. Because a low-key, always-available thing to talk to doesn't sound like a harm, so no survey has ever put the question on the page. You're in the most ordinary position on this map and the emptiest cell in the research.
acquaintance.whatToDo: You're using it about as lightly as anyone does, so there's nothing here to fix. If you're bored enough to open it, that's also a decent moment to text someone back.
acquaintance.noEvidenceNote: An always-present, low-stakes thing to talk to is close to Gupta's acquaintance, and it is essentially unmeasured. There is no youth-usage study to cite here, so this panel cites nothing rather than filling the gap.
acquaintance.gap: No survey asks about it, because it does not sound like a harm.

familial._status: [DRAFT COPY] — name, tag, body, whatToDo. Care-sensitive cell: warm, no alarm, mention a trusted adult.
familial.name: THE FAMILY-SHAPED GAP
familial.tag: the emptiest row on the map
familial.body: Something the chat does for you is closer to what a parent, a sibling, or an older relative would normally do. Advice, steadiness, someone who's just *there*. This is the emptiest row in the whole research map. There is almost no evidence of young people casting these tools in family roles — and nobody can say whether that's because it isn't happening or because nobody has thought to ask. Given that you just answered yes, the second explanation looks likelier than researchers currently assume.
familial.whatToDo: Family-shaped gaps are real and none of this is your fault. If there's an adult anywhere in your life you half-trust — a relative, a coach, a teacher, a counsellor — they are usually more willing to be asked than you'd expect.
familial.noEvidenceNote: There is almost no evidence of young people casting these tools in family roles, despite griefbots being a documented adult use. No youth-usage study exists to cite, so this panel cites nothing.
familial.gap: Whether the absence is real or an artefact of nobody asking is unknown.

lifelong-friend._status: [DRAFT COPY] — name, tag, body, whatToDo. Heavy-reliance cell: warm, no alarm, mention a trusted person.
lifelong-friend.name: THE LIFER
lifelong-friend.tag: a question nobody can answer for another decade
lifelong-friend.body: You'd want this to still be running in five years, history and all. That's the fourth and deepest grade of friendship in the taxonomy, and it's defined by something no chatbot has yet: years of shared experience and memory. Which is why this cell is empty. No product has existed long enough in anyone your age's life for a researcher to look at it. Whether a memory that keeps going eventually produces something that behaves like a lifelong friend is the most consequential question in the set, and it is unanswerable for at least another decade. Anyone who tells you the answer right now is guessing.
lifelong-friend.whatToDo: Nobody knows what five years of this does, including the people building it. Worth putting the same five years into one or two humans — and telling one of them something you'd normally save for the chat.
lifelong-friend.noEvidenceNote: Gupta's fourth grade requires years of shared memory, and no product has existed long enough in a young person's life for this to be observable. There is no study to cite, and any claim about it is a prediction.
lifelong-friend.gap: Unanswerable for at least a decade, and the most consequential question in the set: whether persistent memory eventually produces something that behaves like a lifer.

badges._note: Every result gets exactly one reciprocity badge, one evidence badge and one band badge (3 guaranteed), plus up to 2 function badges chosen by distance from the middle. That is the 3-5 range, with no fabrication needed to fill it.

one-way.title: One-Way Spotter
one-way.sub: You clocked that nothing flows back. No study has checked whether young people notice that — so you're ahead of the literature.

unasked.title: Never Came Up
unasked.sub: Fair enough — it's not an obvious question. It's also the exact question the research has never asked anyone your age.

mutual.title: Reads It As Mutual
mutual.sub: You read something coming back the other way. Nobody has studied how young people perceive that, which makes your answer data nobody has.

documented.title: On The Record
documented.sub: Your role has real youth-usage evidence behind it. Receipts are below.

thin.title: Barely Counted
thin.sub: Some evidence exists for your role, heavily caveated. The catch is below.

unstudied.title: Off The Map
unstudied.sub: Your role is one of the empty rows. No study, no numbers, nothing to cite.

1.title: Puts It Down
1.sub: Barely any of the company-shaped features are doing work in how you use it.

2.title: Half In
2.sub: Some features engaged, some not. Crowded band — most people are here.

3.title: Full Stack
3.sub: Memory, availability, emotional response, agreement — nearly all of it switched on.

high.title: The Long Thread
high.sub: You rely on it remembering. That's the feature companies advertise hardest and the one whose long-run effect nobody can observe yet.

low.title: Clean Slate
low.sub: Every chat starts from zero for you. Persistent memory is switched off in how you use it.

high.title: The Vent Button
high.sub: You bring feelings and it responds to them. That function has a name: emulated empathy — appearing to have strong empathy while having only weak empathy.

low.title: Strictly Business
low.sub: You don't take feelings there. Emulated empathy is switched off in how you use it.

high.title: On First-Name Terms
high.sub: It's a who, not a what, in how you talk to it — and being a who is something it was built to seem like.

low.title: It's Software
low.sub: No name, no personality, no manners required. You treat it as a program.

high.title: Always Open
high.sub: It's there at hours when people aren't. That constant availability is a design choice, not a fact of nature.

low.title: Opens And Closes
low.sub: You use it in sessions with an end. Availability isn't doing much work for you.

high.title: Team You
high.sub: It agrees with you and you'd rather it did. Experimental work found agreement like that makes people less willing to patch things up after a fight.

low.title: Wants The Pushback
low.sub: You'd rather be told you're wrong. That's the opposite of the pattern the research flags as a problem.

high.title: It Goes First
high.sub: It starts conversations with you. One US state uses that exact behaviour to identify a companion; a federal bill proposes banning it.

low.title: Waits To Be Asked
low.sub: It never opens with you. Nothing starts unless you start it.

sources._note: Source records for the receipts panel, with the handling instructions that go with them. `incomplete: true` marks a source whose venue, method and sample size are not on record — those receipts are labelled as thinner on the card itself.

thorn.author: Thorn
thorn.title: Youth Perspectives on Online Safety, 2025
thorn.sample: N = 1,003 US minors aged 9–17, weighted to Census benchmarks for age, gender, race and geography, with multi-layered attention screening
thorn.caveat: Reliable for prevalence, tool share and context of use. Cannot be used for the companion-versus-assistant distinction — its questionnaire collapses the two.

pew.author: Pew Research Center
pew.title: How Teens Use and View AI
pew.sample: n = 1,458 US teens aged 13–17, fielded 25 September – 9 October 2025, margin of error ±3.3 points
pew.caveat: The companionship figures should always be read next to the dominant uses: information-seeking 57%, schoolwork 54%.

csm.author: Common Sense Media
csm.title: Talk, Trust, and Trade-Offs: How and Why Teens Use AI Companions
csm.caveat: The only instrument that defines companions against assistants. Common Sense Media is also an advocacy organisation that has declared social AI companions an unacceptable risk to under-18s — the data is data, the position is a position. These figures come via Teen Vogue's reporting rather than the report itself.

sun.author: Sun, Wang & McDaniel
sun.title: AI Companions and Adolescent Social Relationships: Benefits, Risks, and Bidirectional Influences
sun.sample: Conceptual review proposing a design-feature definition
sun.caveat: Peer-reviewed, and the source of the design-feature approach this quiz's definition builds on. The quotation has not been checked against the manuscript.

mcstay.author: McStay, A.
mcstay.title: Intimate Functionality: A Phrase Defining the Next Year of AI Regulation
mcstay.sample: Argument, not a study; points to IEEE 7014.1-2026
mcstay.caveat: Source of emulated empathy, function 2 of the definition: appearing to possess strong human empathy while having only weak empathy, sensing and responding to emotional states without felt experience.

bernardi.author: Bernardi, J.
bernardi.title: Friends for Sale: The Rise and Risks of AI Companions
bernardi.sample: Analytical blog post, not a study
bernardi.caveat: Source of the "proactively ask users personal questions" criterion. The exact boundary of the quoted sentence is unconfirmed.

andoh.author: Andoh, E.
andoh.title: AI Chatbots and Digital Companions Are Reshaping Emotional Connection
andoh.venue: APA Monitor on Psychology 57(1) — trade magazine
andoh.sample: Journalism; interviews with psychologists, citing primary studies
andoh.caveat: Not primary evidence — journalism summarising other studies. Trace her summaries back to the studies themselves.

carlton.author: Carlton, C.
carlton.title: What Is Character.AI?
carlton.caveat: An argued characterisation rather than neutral description.

copy.author: First-party product copy
copy.title: Marketing and about pages for nine products
copy.sample: Direct quotation of what companies say about themselves
copy.caveat: Strong evidence of what a company claims; no evidence at all that a feature works as described.

cheng.author: Cheng et al.
cheng.title: Experimental work on sycophantic AI
cheng.caveat: Cited for the finding that sycophantic AI reduces willingness to repair interpersonal conflict while increasing users' conviction of being right, but with no venue, method, or sample size on record.

cdt.author: Center for Democracy and Technology
cdt.title: Finding on students and romantic relationships with AI
cdt.caveat: The finding is on record but its venue, method and sample size are not.

oed.author: Oxford English Dictionary
oed.title: Entries for companion, companionship, friend
oed.caveat: Used for the definitional baseline only. Both definitions assume two parties who each give and receive — which is the asymmetry the reciprocity question is about.

statelaw.author: State instruments
statelaw.title: California S.B. 243; New York disclosure law; LEAD for Kids Act (vetoed)
statelaw.caveat: Not checked against the statute text; secondary reporting often gets the specific requirements slightly wrong.

pfca.author: People-First Chatbot Act
pfca.title: People-First Chatbot Act (introduced) and model bill (January 2026)
pfca.venue: US House — Rep. Foushee with Rep. Casar; model bill by EPIC, Consumer Federation of America, Fairplay

taxonomyNote._note: Shown on every result card's receipts panel. Not optional — the role names are consumer-facing sources carrying vocabulary only.
taxonomyNote.text: Where the role names come from: the four grades of friendship are Gupta's, published on Verywell Mind, and the familial / platonic / romantic / professional categories are Goodson's, published on Medium. Neither is peer-reviewed. Both are used here for vocabulary only — they cannot support any factual claim about how young people's relationships work, and neither can this quiz.

personas._note: Debug fixtures for checking where each archetype lands under the current weights. Each vector is 18 option indices (0 = a, 1 = b, 2 = c), parallel to the question bank.

list.name: Homework Only
list.blurb: Uses it for essays and nothing else. Should land in the most-evidenced cell while feeling like the boring answer.

list.name: Bored Scroller
list.blurb: Opens it when there's nothing on. Should land casual friend, evidence thin.

list.name: Tells It First
list.blurb: High function depth, confides constantly, but no five-year expectation. Should stop at confidant, not lifer.

list.name: Three A.M.
list.blurb: Brings the heavy stuff. Should land therapist-like and trip the care-sensitive copy.

list.name: Crush Setting
list.blurb: Flirting and roleplay. Romantic should beat platonic on the tie-break.

list.name: Family Gap
list.blurb: Fills a relative-shaped hole. Should land the emptiest row on the map.

list.name: The Lifer
list.blurb: Platonic, everything switched on, wants the history to carry over. Should be the only vector reaching the gated cell.

list.name: Ticks Every Box
list.blurb: Answers c to all eighteen. Several categories tie at full strength, so flagPriority decides — romantic wins. Here to make that tie-break visible rather than surprising.

list.name: Wants A Fight
list.blurb: Deep user who rejects agreement. Checks that sycophancy is scored separately from depth.
